zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. Dataset: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Used as a vocabulary aid, not as a replacement transcription; this copy’s spelling and typography remain scan-grounded.

lines.note: Completes the preceding page's definition of capital put into something. Kono sakuji no irime begins an example about the expense of building work; em is running text here, unlike the preceding page's repeated catchword.
Gives that expense as ten kanme; the Portuguese starts the explanation of what was spent. The close printed ſegaſtou spacing is retained.
The dictionary translates the construction expense as one thousand taels. This is the source's own equivalence, not a modern currency conversion.

Irimidare means entering in a mixed crowd or throng. Enlargement supports printed romania, with n, although romaria is the natural Portuguese comparison; the anomalous form is retained, and de tropel confirms the intended crowd sense.
De tropel completes the description of entering in a crowd or rush, closing the irimidare entry.

runs.text: Bolinhos torrados, ou aßados em pa

lines.note: Irimochi denotes roasted or baked cakes. Panella is divided as pa / nella without a printed end hyphen.
Completes panella, the pot or pan in which the cakes are heated; doubled ll is preserved.

runs.text: Ienro q̃ ẽtra pera erdar a caſa do ſogro.

lines.note: Irimuko is a son-in-law who enters the father-in-law's household to inherit it. Portuguese Ienro uses consonantal I, while q̃ and ẽtra preserve printed abbreviations.
Irioo, alternatively yerioo, denotes the cost of having clothing made. Custo has a t rather than OCR l; the circumflexes on both Japanese forms remain as printed.

runs.text: do que ſe talha, ou faz pera alguem. ¶

lines.note: Completes vestido and specifies cutting or making it for someone. Co- begins kono in the Japanese example below.

runs.text: no qirumonouo xitatçuruni iriô, l, yeriô

lines.note: The example asks about the expense of making this garment. Qirumono is the historical kirumono form; it is not replaced with modern kimono.

Nanboo hodo iroozu asks how much will be needed. The damaged final vowel of Quanto retains an oval trace compatible with o and the Portuguese question, rather than the OCR's e; the reading is usable but the impression is weak.

runs.text: de gasto pera fazer eſte vestido?

lines.note: Completes the question about the expense required to make the garment. The question mark and locally supplied st spellings remain visible source features.
Iriki denotes power and authority. The Portuguese reads Poder, not OCR Pider.
Iritsuke is the transitive action of making something stick while roasting it. The headword begins with capital I, not lowercase l; fogo continues below.
Completes fogo torrandoa, specifying the action of roasting over a fire. The following entry supplies the corresponding intransitive sticking sense.
Iritsuki is the intransitive counterpart: something sticks as it roasts. The principal part ita remains unexpanded.
Completes the roasting circumstance, with the source's grave accent in està and provisional st allograph retained.
Iriumi is an inlet or arm of the sea. The separate entry is not merged with the closely related iriye below.

runs.text: Enſeada, ou braço de mar que entra pella

lines.note: Iriye likewise denotes an inlet, here explained as an arm of the sea extending inland. The printed doubled l in pella is preserved.
Completes the inland extension of the inlet, not a separate geographical term.
Irizacaxino is described as a particular escabeche-like sauce or condiment. The unusual Japanese sequence is preserved from this impression rather than replaced with a modern culinary name.
Iro means colour; iro wo ushinau is losing one's colour. The faint initial I and the r in Irouo are visible, correcting OCR ro and Itouo; vxinǒ keeps the source's long-vowel notation.
Completes perder as cores, then gives iro wo kaete isamuru, admonishing with a changed expression. Irouo again has r, not OCR t.

runs.text: prender a alguem, ou dar lhe conſelho por va

lines.note: Completes reprender and adds giving someone counsel by various means. Varias is divided as va / rias without an end hyphen.

Completes the counsel gloss, then introduces iro wo naosu, restoring or changing the complexion. The initial n of nauoſu is supported by the scan and the repeated nauoxi forms below, unlike OCR uauoſu.

runs.text: cor do roſto, ou oſembrante que dantes estaua

lines.note: The object is the face's colour or expression, previously altered. The close oſembrante spacing is retained without changing the meaning to a different word.
Completes the description of a disturbed or angry expression. Iro nauo- begins the related noun for changing colour, developed below as a clothing custom.
Completes iro naoshi and illustrates iro naoshi wo suru. The Portuguese introduces a change of clothing colour rather than another facial-expression example.

runs.text: cor dos vestidos como fazẽ os meninos de vin

lines.note: The dictionary begins its examples of changing clothing colour with infants at twenty or thirty days. Fazẽ is abbreviated, and vinte is physically divided without a terminal hyphen.

runs.text: te, ou trinta dias por diante, os que caſão de

lines.note: Completes twenty or thirty days onward, then turns to newly married people. De begins depois on the next row without a printed hyphen.

runs.text: pois de dous, ou tres dias, & os que tirão o dò

lines.note: Specifies two or three days after marriage and then those ending mourning. Dò is the source's accented word for mourning, not an omitted longer form.

runs.text: por reſpeito dalgum defunto. Todos eſtes deſpẽ

lines.note: Completes mourning for a deceased person, then says that all the groups just listed take off a garment. Deſpẽ preserves the abbreviation for despem.

runs.text: vestido de cor branca, & ſe vestem de vari-

lines.note: The garment removed is white, and the replacement clothing is of various colours. The source describes the custom; vari- continues below.
Completes varias cores and closes the extended iro-naoshi clothing explanation.
A separate iro entry denotes sensuality. Iro ni fukeru means giving oneself over to it, as the divided Portuguese entregar-se explains.
Completes entregar-se à sensualidade, then begins iro wo omonzuru. The visibly extra vowel in printed ſenſualiadade is retained; the normal form appears again two rows below.
Completes omonzuru with the same sensuality gloss, then introduces iro wo konomu. Dar begins dar-se on the next row without a visible end hyphen.
Completes the Portuguese expression for indulging in sensuality and adds irogonomi wo suru as another equivalent construction.
Idem applies the preceding sensuality gloss to irogonomi wo suru, closing the entry.
Irokashi means drying by heat. The principal part aita reflects the historical inflection and is not modernized to ashita.
Cha wo irokasu is equated with cha wo hashiyagasu, drying tea. The scan includes the paragraph marker omitted by OCR and a comma after i; both are restored on the same physical row.

runs.text: Secar, ou enxugar o Cha que esta humido. No

lines.note: The Portuguese explains drying damp tea, then begins a regional usage statement. No accent is supplied to the weakly printed esta without secure graphic evidence.
Completes No Cami se diz, stating that hashiyagasu is used in the Cami region. Cami and the quoted verb belong to a Portuguese regional explanation, not a new headword.
Iroko means a fish scale; iroko wo fuku is illustrated by removing the scales. The source's i- initial is not regularized to modern uroko.
Directly translates the example as scaling a fish, completing the iroko entry.

runs.text: Couſa de figura triangular, ou de

lines.note: Irokogata describes a scale-like triangular shape. The damaged initial still supports Irocogata, not OCR rucogata; triangular has n, not r in the middle.
Three corners completes and confirms the triangular-shape gloss. The scan reads tres cantos, not OCR tre centos; this is the final left-column body row.
Irodori means painting or colouring in several colours. Varias is divided as va / rias without a printed hyphen; the principal part otta is retained.
Completes varias cores and begins mokuzoo wo irodori kazaru, colouring and adorning a wooden statue. The caron on the Japanese long o is visible.

runs.text: Pintar de varias tintas, & ornar a eſ-

lines.note: Completes kazaru and translates the colouring and adornment of the statue. Eſ- begins estatua below.
Completes estatua, the object of both painting and ornamentation in the preceding example.
Irofushi no mono is explained as male or female travelling entertainers. The abbreviated plural Homẽs begins the description continued below.

runs.text: molheres q̃ deſcorrem por diuerſas partes a re-

lines.note: These people travel through different places to entertain. The source's molheres, q̃, and deſcorrem are retained without modernizing their spelling or expanding the abbreviation.

runs.text: crear a gente com bailos, canto, &c.

lines.note: Completes recrear and specifies dances and singing as the means of entertaining people. Bailos is the printed noun, not a spelling to be replaced from modern usage.
Irogonomi is sensuality or lust, corresponding to the related iro expressions in the left column.

Iroi denotes having dealings with something or interfering. Printed deuer is interpreted through the following de ver com example, not as a gloss about moral obligation; its close spelling remains unchanged.
Mono ni iroo illustrates involvement with something. The Portuguese explicitly gives ter de ver com, clarifying the preceding compressed deuer.
Completes alguma cousa, the object of the involvement described in the example.
Iroiro has both the literal many-colours sense and the generalized sense of various kinds or manners. The second gloss continues below.
Completes de muitas maneiras and illustrates iroiro ni kawaru, changing in many ways. Mudar continues with the reflexive pronoun on the next row.
Completes mudar-se de muitas maneiras, the translation of the variation example. No end hyphen is supplied to the preceding Mudar.
Iromeki is glossed as colour shining or becoming conspicuous. The historical principal part eita and italic Vt are retained.
The example describes appearing with a conspicuous or shining aspect. A- begins Portuguese aparecendo below; no source label is inserted after the Japanese sentence.
Completes aparecendo, rendering the example as appearing in a shining manner. The source itself supplies this interpretation of the Japanese sentence.

runs.text: Outra opinião differente no diſputar. Vt,

lines.note: Iron is a divergent opinion in debate. The double f in differente and the unaccented headword are preserved.
Iron machimachi nari says that the opinions differ. The Portuguese disputa is divided as diſ / puta without a printed end hyphen.
Completes disputa and states that the views expressed in it are diverse, closing the disagreement example.
Iro nai hito is equated with sugenai hito, an unresponsive or curt person. The faint but present initial I is restored rather than keeping OCR ronai.
Adds harsh or brusque to the personal description, then illustrates saying something curtly. Di- begins dizer below.

runs.text: zer algũa couſa riſpida, ou ſecamente.

lines.note: Completes dizer, saying something brusque or in a dry manner. The scan has zer, not the OCR's zir.
Ironaoshi refers back to Iro and its clothing-colour explanation. The cross-reference Iro is upright, distinct from italic Vide, and is a Japanese citation within the Latin apparatus.
Ironashi describes something without colour. It is a separate literal colour entry beside the preceding figurative descriptions of brusqueness.
Ironikuu is an adverbial expression for speaking brusquely. The headword begins with I, not OCR F, and its final caron is retained.
Iro nikuu moosu or yuu means speaking in a curt, dry fashion. The spaced Iro nicǔ is left as printed rather than joined to match the headword.
Restates the example as speaking in that manner, completing the adverbial gloss.
Irori is a hearth in which a fire is made. The direct gloss is retained without substituting a modern stove description.

runs.text: Couſa illuminada, ou pintada de diuer-

lines.note: Iroye denotes something coloured or painted in different colours. The divided diversas leads into a figurative speech-related sense below.
Completes diversas cores and introduces kotoba no iroe, verbal colouring or ornament. Permet marks the figurative extension in the Portuguese apparatus.

runs.text: Ornato de palauras, ou compoſição, & afeite,

lines.note: Explains verbal ornament, composition and adornment. Enlargement supports afeite with a narrow i before t and a final comma, not OCR afette followed by a full stop; the sentence continues into the manner of speaking below.
The ornament is in gentle, measured speech. Coto- starts a contrasting example of speaking without such verbal colouring.
Completes kotoba no iroe mo noo yuu, speaking without that ornament. The negative nǒ is confirmed by the Portuguese contrast, speaking brusquely.
Secamente completes the curt or dry manner of speech, closing the figurative iroye example.
The separate verbal iroye means painting or colouring. The source supplies its principal forms rather than merging it with the preceding noun.
Completes varias cores, the many-coloured painting sense of the verb.
Irozzuki means acquiring colour. Aki ni na begins the seasonal example; no hyphen is added after na merely because nareba continues below.
Completes aki ni nareba, when autumn comes, and says that leaves on all sides change colour. The faint e in reba fits the visible open form and the conditional construction, correcting OCR roba.

runs.text: Outono por todas as partes as folhas das aruo-

lines.note: Begins the Portuguese account of autumn leaves everywhere. Aruores uses the historical u/v spelling and is divided at the physical edge.

runs.text: res ſe còram fazendoſe vermelhas, ou amarel

lines.note: Completes arvores and says that the leaves turn red or yellow. Amarellas is divided without a printed end hyphen.
Completes amarellas, then gives konomi ga irozzuku, fruit taking on colour as it ripens. Sazonar continues with the reflexive pronoun below.
Explains the ripening of fruit and introduces ine ga irozzuku, the corresponding maturation of rice. The printed fruita spelling is retained.

runs.text: Sazonarſe a ſeara do arroz ja eſpigado.

lines.note: Completes the rice example and explains it as the ripening of a rice crop already in ear. No modern accent is added to ja.

Iru is labelled a defective verb and illustrated by ha ga iru, with itta as the alternative past form below. Fresh enlarged inspection in the second pass shows two t types in the lemma as well, correcting the bootstrap ita. The Portuguese concerns teeth becoming blunted or set on edge, not entering or roasting.

runs.text: Botaremſe os dentes como quãdo ſe come

lines.note: Completes the past-form alternative and describes teeth becoming blunted or set on edge, as when eating sour unripe things. The close Botaremſe spelling is retained; the weak final vowel of printed comi remains a graphic caveat rather than being silently modernized to come.
Specifies green or unripe and sour foods, completing the teeth example. The final word reads azedas, not OCR azedao.
Iruka is glossed by the Portuguese cetacean name toninha, broadly a porpoise or dolphin here; the brief entry does not support a narrower modern species identification.

Irui means clothing. This genuine final dictionary entry was merged by the OCR bootstrap with the adjacent signature and catchword; it is restored to column 2 under its existing ID, with a body-line crop.
